original_query: SELECT t2.SAL, t2.EXPR1, t5.EXPR2, t9.EXPR3 FROM (SELECT SAL, SUM(COMM) AS EXPR1 FROM EMP GROUP BY SAL) AS t2 INNER JOIN (SELECT SAL, AVG(COMM) AS EXPR2 FROM (SELECT SAL, COMM FROM EMP GROUP BY SAL, COMM) AS t4 GROUP BY SAL) AS t5 ON t2.SAL IS NOT DISTINCT FROM t5.SAL INNER JOIN (SELECT SAL, SUM(SAL) AS EXPR3 FROM (SELECT SAL FROM EMP GROUP BY SAL) AS t8 GROUP BY SAL) AS t9 ON t2.SAL IS NOT DISTINCT FROM t9.SAL
rewritten_query:
SELECT SAL,
       SUM(COMM) AS EXPR1,
       AVG(DISTINCT COMM) AS EXPR2,
       SAL AS EXPR3
FROM EMP
GROUP BY SAL

rewrite_suggestion.produced_suggestion: The nested subquery t4 (GROUP BY SAL, COMM followed by AVG(COMM) GROUP BY SAL) computes the average of distinct COMM values per SAL, which is equivalent to AVG(DISTINCT COMM). This removes one subquery level.

Subquery t9 (SUM(SAL) over a single distinct SAL per group) degenerates: for non-null SAL it equals SAL, and for null SAL SUM yields NULL, which equals SAL. Thus t9.EXPR3 can be replaced with SAL, removing an entire subquery and join.

All three derived tables group the same EMP table by SAL and always produce exactly one row per distinct SAL (including NULL), so the IS NOT DISTINCT FROM joins never filter rows. All three aggregates can be merged into a single GROUP BY SAL over one scan of EMP.

With EMP at 45M rows, the original plan performs three parallel sequential scans, multiple aggregations, sorts, and nested-loop joins. A single grouped aggregation over one scan drastically reduces I/O and CPU. No CTE is needed since there is no repeated computation after merging.
